title: MOS I/V Characteristics
intro: The drain current of a long-channel MOSFET follows a square law above threshold. This page derives it, defines the regions of operation and introduces transconductance (Razavi, Section 2.2).

blocks.text: Threshold voltage

Raise the gate of an NMOS from zero with source, drain and bulk grounded. First the positive gate repels holes from the surface, leaving a depletion region of fixed negative ions; no current can flow because there are no mobile carriers. The gate oxide and the depletion region act like two capacitors in series dividing the gate voltage. As $V_G$ rises the surface potential rises until electrons from the source flood in and form a thin inversion layer (the channel) joining source and drain. Beyond that point extra gate charge is mirrored almost entirely by more channel electrons, while the depletion charge stays roughly constant.
Turn-on is gradual, so $V_{TH}$ needs a definition. The physics definition is the gate voltage at which the surface is as strongly n-type as the bulk is p-type, giving

Here $\Phi_{MS}$ is the gate-substrate work-function difference, $N_{sub}$ the substrate doping and $C_{ox}$ the oxide capacitance per unit area ($\epsilon_{ox}/t_{ox}$; about $17\text{ fF/}\mu\text{m}^2$ for $t_{ox} = 2\text{ nm}$, scaling inversely with thickness). The natural value is rarely what circuits want, so fabs adjust it with a threshold-adjust implant near the surface: a thin p+ layer raises $V_{TH}$. For a PMOS everything is mirrored: a sufficiently negative $V_{GS}$ forms a hole channel and $V_{TH}$ is negative. For the rest of the chapter assume the device switches on abruptly at $V_{GS} = V_{TH}$.

Each curve rises steeply, bends over where VDS equals the overdrive voltage, and then continues almost flat with a slight upward slope. A dashed red parabola joins the bending points and separates the triode region on the left from the saturation region on the right.

blocks.text: Deriving the I/V curve

Two facts give the whole characteristic. First, a current is charge density times velocity: if a bar carries $Q_d$ coulombs per metre moving at $v$ metres per second, $I = Q_d v$. Second, above threshold the channel charge per unit length is set by the gate voltage in excess of threshold. With the drain at $V_{DS}$ the channel potential $V(x)$ rises from 0 at the source to $V_{DS}$ at the drain, so the local charge is

Electron velocity is $\mu_n E = \mu_n\, dV/dx$, so $I_D = W C_{ox}[V_{GS} - V(x) - V_{TH}]\mu_n\, dV/dx$. Since $I_D$ is the same everywhere along the channel, integrate $x$ from 0 to $L$ and $V$ from 0 to $V_{DS}$:

Each curve is a parabola in $V_{DS}$ with its peak at $V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_{TH}$. The quantity $V_{GS} - V_{TH}$ is the overdrive voltage $V_{ov}$; the region $V_{DS} \le V_{ov}$ is the triode (linear) region. The integration assumed $\mu_n$ and $V_{TH}$ do not vary along the channel, which short-channel devices violate (see Short-Channel Effects and Device Models).
Deep triode: a voltage-controlled resistor
For $V_{DS} \ll 2(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$ the squared term is negligible, the current is linear in $V_{DS}$, and the channel is a resistor whose value the gate sets:

Unlike a bipolar transistor, a MOSFET can be fully on while carrying no current at all ($V_{DS} = 0$). Gate-controlled resistors are used for tuning (for example adjusting an oscillator frequency) and, as switches, throughout sampled-data circuits.
Saturation and pinch-off

When $V_{DS}$ exceeds $V_{ov}$ the charge density $Q_d(x)$ reaches zero before the drain: the channel is pinched off. Electrons reaching the pinch-off point are swept across the depletion region to the drain by its strong field, and the current stops growing. Repeating the integral only up to the pinch-off point $L'$, where the channel voltage is $V_{GS} - V_{TH}$, gives

blocks.tex: I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L'}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^2, \qquad V_{GS} = \sqrt{\frac{2I_D}{\mu_n C_{ox} W/L}} + V_{TH}
blocks.caption: Saturation (square law); with $L' \approx L$ the current is independent of $V_{DS}$

blocks.text: The minimum $V_{DS}$ for saturation, $V_{D,sat} = V_{GS} - V_{TH}$, is voltage the circuit must leave across the device; every overdrive chosen costs that much of the signal headroom. A saturated device with fixed $V_{GS}$ is a current source between drain and source. For a PMOS the equations carry a minus sign (current defined into the drain while holes flow out), with $V_{GS}$, $V_{DS}$ and $V_{TH}$ all negative when it is on; hole mobility is roughly half of electron mobility, so a PMOS of equal size carries about half the current.

blocks.text: Regions of operation

blocks.alt: A plane with VGS on the horizontal axis and VDS on the vertical axis. A dashed vertical line at VTH separates the off region on the left. From VTH a solid diagonal line VDS = VGS minus VTH rises to the right. The region above the diagonal is labelled saturation, the region below it triode.
blocks.caption: Regions on the VGS-VDS plane. For a fixed VDS, increasing VGS eventually moves the device from saturation into triode.

items: Saturation: $V_{GS} > V_{TH}$ and $V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_{TH}$. Amplifiers bias their devices here.

A shortcut that needs no source voltage: an NMOS is saturated when its gate is less than one threshold above its drain ($V_G - V_D < V_{TH}$), because then the gate cannot invert the channel at the drain end. A PMOS is saturated when $V_D - V_G < |V_{TH}|$. You must still know which terminal is the drain.

blocks.text: Transconductance
Amplifiers care about how a change of gate voltage changes the current. The transconductance, defined in saturation at constant $V_{DS}$, has three equivalent forms:

blocks.tex: g_m = \frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}} = \mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH}) = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_D} = \frac{2 I_D}{V_{GS}-V_{TH}}

blocks.text: Each form answers a different question. At fixed $W/L$, $g_m$ grows linearly with overdrive and as $\sqrt{I_D}$; at fixed current, $g_m$ falls as the overdrive rises, so high $g_m$ for little current calls for a small overdrive and a wide device. The square-root form suggests $g_m$ can grow without limit by widening the device at fixed current; it cannot, because the overdrive eventually approaches zero and the device enters subthreshold (see Second-Order Effects). Note that saturation $g_m$ equals $1/R_{on}$ of the same device in deep triode at the same overdrive. For a PMOS, $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)|I_D|}$ with the same magnitudes.
In triode the transconductance is $\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)V_{DS}$, which shrinks as $V_{DS}$ falls. That is the main reason amplifying devices are kept in saturation.

Watch where each curve leaves the dashed parabola: that is $V_{DS} = V_{ov}$, the triode/saturation boundary. In saturation the curves are nearly flat; their slope is set by $\lambda$. Raising $V_{GS}$ lifts the curve with square-law spacing.

At a fixed $W/L$, $g_m$ grows only as the square root of $I_D$, so doubling the current buys just 41 percent more $g_m$. Doubling $W/L$ instead raises $g_m$ by the same factor at fixed current with no power cost, at the price of more capacitance.

blocks.title: A simple bias point
blocks.text: An NMOS has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 200\,\mu\text{A/V}^2$, $W/L = 10$, $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$ and $\lambda = 0$. For $V_{GS} = 0.8\text{ V}$ and $V_{DS} = 1\text{ V}$ find $I_D$ and $g_m$. Then find $I_D$ for $V_{GS} = 0.8\text{ V}$ and $V_{DS} = 0.1\text{ V}$.
blocks.hint: Check whether the drain-source voltage exceeds the overdrive first.
solution: $V_{ov} = 0.4\text{ V}$ and $V_{DS} = 1\text{ V} > V_{ov}$, so the device is saturated.
$\mu_n C_{ox} W/L = 2\text{ mA/V}^2$, so $I_D = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot (0.4\text{ V})^2 = 160\,\mu\text{A}$.
With $V_{DS} = 0.1\text{ V} < V_{ov}$ the device is in triode: $I_D = 2\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot (0.4 \cdot 0.1 - 0.1^2/2)\text{ V}^2 = 2\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot 0.035\text{ V}^2 = 70\,\mu\text{A}$.

blocks.title: Saturation or triode?
blocks.text: A transistor has $V_G = 1.5\text{ V}$, $V_S = 0$, $V_D = 1.0\text{ V}$, $V_{TH} = 0.5\text{ V}$. Which region is it in? What if $V_D = 0.6\text{ V}$?
solution: $V_D = 1.0\text{ V}$ gives $V_{DS} = V_{ov}$: the edge of saturation (equivalently $V_G - V_D = 0.5\text{ V} = V_{TH}$). $V_D = 0.6\text{ V}$ gives $V_{DS} < V_{ov}$: triode.
blocks.answer: Edge of saturation at $V_D = 1.0\text{ V}$; triode at $V_D = 0.6\text{ V}$.

blocks.title: What the 2ID/Vov form tells you
blocks.text: Two designs carry the same $I_D = 100\,\mu\text{A}$. One uses $V_{ov} = 0.2\text{ V}$, the other $V_{ov} = 0.4\text{ V}$. Compare $g_m$, and say what you pay for the higher one.
solution: $g_m = 2I_D/V_{ov}$: $1\text{ mS}$ for the first design, $0.5\text{ mS}$ for the second.
At fixed current $W/L \propto 1/V_{ov}^2$, so the low-overdrive design needs a $W/L$ four times larger: more area and more capacitance. (It does gain headroom, since it needs less $V_{D,sat}$.)
blocks.answer: 1 mS versus 0.5 mS; the higher $g_m$ costs four times the $W/L$.

blocks.title: A PMOS bias point
blocks.text: A PMOS with $\mu_p C_{ox} = 80\,\mu\text{A/V}^2$, $W/L = 25$ and $|V_{TH}| = 0.45\text{ V}$ has its source at 1.2 V, gate at 0.5 V and drain at 0.6 V. Find its region, $|I_D|$ and $g_m$.
solution: $V_{SG} = 0.7\text{ V}$, so the overdrive is $0.7 - 0.45 = 0.25\text{ V}$. $V_{SD} = 0.6\text{ V} > 0.25\text{ V}$: saturated. (Check with the shortcut: $V_D - V_G = 0.1\text{ V} < |V_{TH}|$.)

blocks.title: Transconductance in triode
blocks.text: A device has $\mu_n C_{ox} W/L = 2\text{ mA/V}^2$, $V_{GS} = 0.9\text{ V}$ and $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$. Find $g_m$ in saturation and at $V_{DS} = 0.2\text{ V}$.
solution: At $V_{DS} = 0.2\text{ V} < 0.5\text{ V}$ the device is in triode and $g_m = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)V_{DS} = 0.4\text{ mS}$, less than half.
blocks.answer: 1 mS in saturation, 0.4 mS in triode.
